title: Staged degradation red-team & eviction theorycraft
topics: telemetry signals and SLO escape hatches
summary: Theorycraft session to align engineering, SRE, and product on eviction behavior during high-concurrency tails and to design a red-team tabletop for staged degradation. Outcome: agree on three telemetry signals, a set of runbook changes, and owners for a 48-hour chaos exercise.
next_steps: Priya: draft red-team script and failure matrix and share by 2026-11-09
Lina: add KV cache eviction counters to export and dashboard by 2026-11-08
Marcus: prototype staged-response policy (disk-backed fallback + model downgrade) and demo 2026-11-12
Jordan: coordinate calendar invite for 2026-11-16 tabletop and invite legal/compliance
action_items: Priya Raman | Write red-team failure matrix + script | 2026-11-09
Lina Torres | Instrument cache eviction and miss-rate metrics | 2026-11-08
Marcus Chen | Implement staged-response policy prototype on canary cluster | 2026-11-12
Aisha Patel | Prepare stakeholder impact matrix and rollback comms draft | 2026-11-10
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (PM): OK, starting. Welcome everyone. The goal for today is to theorycraft staged degradation, like uh, what happens when eviction storms hit KV cache during a traffic spike and how we run a red-team tabletop for it. Say your name and quick role.
[00:28] Priya (SRE): Priya, SRE, focus on oncall and observability.
[00:33] Marcus (Eng Lead): Marcus, runtime. I've got the quant kernels and batching work in flight.
[00:38] Lina (Runtime): Lina, cache and memory teams.
[00:41] Aisha (Eng Manager): Aisha, ops and capacity.
[00:45] Diego (Ops): Diego, infra, network and region failover.
[00:50] Evan (Oncall): Evan, covering paging and runbooks.
[00:55] Jordan: Cool. Quick context: we saw two close calls last quarter where eviction churn amplified token latency. We did mitigations but we still lack a clear staged-degradation playbook. Today I want to walk through failure modes, list telemetry hooks, and pick owners for a red-team sim.
[01:15] Marcus: To add, some of those incidents were correlated with large prefixes plus model lock contention, which made KV warming slower. Our continuous batching made bursty tails worse in a couple paths.
[01:30] Priya: Yup, and on top of that the autoscaler reacted slowly because it was looking at CPU not at effective queue depth, so we hit a latency SLO for a few minutes.
[01:43] Lina: Also, the eviction policy currently is LRU-ish but under large sequence-length variance it ends up evicting keys we need for warm starts.
[01:53] Jordan: Right. Let's enumerate concrete failure modes. I'll capture them and then we do a tabletop scenario for each. First list?
[02:05] Speaker 6: Eviction storm after a traffic burst with many long-context requests—cache becomes useless for a cohort.
[02:12] Priya: Model downgrade policy not kicking because routing still selected high-precision variant, so cost stayed high and throughput dropped.
[02:21] Marcus: Kernel fallback occurred but increased latency; we had cascading queue buildup.
[02:28] Diego: Region B started steering traffic to Region A causing cross-region KV miss overhead.
[02:34] Jordan: Good. Now telemetry. What signals do we want to treat as gating?
[02:40] Priya: Eviction rate per pool, miss rate for KV per model shard, and average time-to-warm (time from first token to effective cache hit).
[02:50] Lina: Also queue depth per serving thread, and a percent of requests hitting fallback kernels.
[02:56] Marcus: Add tail-p99.9 token latency. That was the thing that bubbled on the dashboard.
[03:03] Evan: From oncall perspective we need a synthesized signal: correlated increase in eviction-rate + rising queue depth + p99.9 spike — that should escalate to manual rollback or model downgrade.
[03:16] Jordan: OK so three immediate telemetry gates: eviction-rate, kv-miss-rate, and p99.9. We'll set thresholds later.
[03:24] Priya: For the red-team script, I'm thinking staged injects: step 1 is synthetic burst of long-context, step 2 is concurrent small bursts to exhaust concurrency, step 3 is region failover.
[03:36] Lina: If we do step 1 we should also simulate cold-start keys so we see time-to-warm impact.
[03:41] Marcus: For step 2, throttle the kernel selection path to force falling back to slower kernels, so we see queue effects.
[03:49] Diego: And we can flip routing policy to send 30% more to canary to exercise routing fallback.
[03:55] Jordan: Good. Let's talk mitigations and runbook actions at each stage. If telemetry gate trips, what do we do?
[04:05] Evan: First action is increase retention for prefix cache on the impacted pool if possible — that's a config flip. Second, divert non-critical traffic to a lower-cost variant or spike buffer.
[04:17] Marcus: We can also enable an emergency model-variant that uses larger batching and quantized kernels, cheaper but slightly lower quality. Need a quick way to flip that per customer or globally.
[04:28] Priya: Oncall should run a pre-canned script that reduces acceptance tokens for long-context requests and lower max concurrency for certain routes.
[04:37] Lina: There's also the option of using disk-backed KV for cold keys — read-through cache to reduce latency spikes when cache is emptied. But that changes IO profile.
[04:46] Diego: Disk-backed will increase tail latencies for the first few tokens; we need to define which tiers get that fallback. Enterprise customers maybe keep in-memory only.
[04:57] Jordan: Right, so staged-response policy could be: 1) in-memory retention increase -> 2) model downgrade/routing -> 3) disk-backed read-through for low tier -> 4) global throttling.
[05:11] Aisha: Need to ensure legal/compliance OKs: disk fallback may interact with data residency and ephemeral keys. We should involve compliance for the tabletop.
[05:22] Jordan: Noted. We'll invite compliance.
[05:24] Marcus: Technical detail: enabling disk read-through requires our cache layer to serialize KV entries and we need to verify encryption at rest. That'll add work.
[05:34] Priya: Let's sketch the red-team success criteria. We want to observe that telemetry gates trigger the automated steps, and that the system converges within 3 minutes to below p99.9 threshold, or we successfully roll back.
[05:46] Jordan: Good metric. And we'll measure recovery time and impact to cost and quality.
[05:52] Evan: Also ensure runbook pages include exact dashboard links, query IDs, and command-line toggles — oncall hate hunting for them.
[06:01] Lina: On instrumentation, I need clarity on the kv hit/miss logic. Right now we emit a per-shard counter but no per-model breakdown. Please confirm we need per-model shard.
[06:11] Priya: Yes per-model shard is necessary. Otherwise we can't tell if it's one hot model causing churn.
[06:17] Marcus: There's another dimension: sequence-length percentiles per route. If we can tag requests with expected seq length bucket it's easier to route to specialized pools.
[06:28] Jordan: Great. Let's move to simulated tabletop flow. We'll take the eviction-storm scenario and role-play. I'll be incident commander.
[06:36] Jordan: Step 0: inject long-context spike. Step 1: eviction rate crosses threshold. What does SRE do?
[06:44] Priya: Pager goes to oncall. Oncall checks dashboard. If the synthesized signal (eviction high + p99.9 high) is true, declare P1. Then runbook step: increase retention, throttle long-context.
[06:55] Evan: If comms needed, trigger the incident-template to customers on affected routes. We have pre-approved language in drafts.
[07:03] Aisha: For internal comms, product and sales should be notified if enterprise tiers are affected. Need an escalation matrix.
[07:11] Jordan: We'll add that. Now consider a failure in the mitigation: retention increase didn't help because memory saturated. Then what?
[07:20] Marcus: Next step is immediate model downgrade routing to cheaper model variant and enable batching optimizations.
[07:26] Lina: But if we switch model variant mid-request we risk response inconsistency. Maybe we should only route new requests to variant, not mid-flight.
[07:34] Diego: That implies we need a graceful drain. We should plan for ripple windows where new traffic goes to fallback.
[07:41] Priya: We have to balance quality vs latency; define per-customer SLAs and fallbacks.
[07:47] Jordan: OK. We're outlining policy. Let's capture a short decision tree draft in the doc.
[07:53] Speaker 6: Question — what about the autoscaler tuning? We said it keyed on CPU. Can we quickly add queue-depth as a scaler metric?
[08:01] Marcus: We can, but needs evaluation — queue depth is noisy. Maybe use smoothed p95 queue depth and scale thresholds.
[08:10] Priya: Also use request concurrency per shard, that's more direct.
[08:14] Jordan: Excellent. Now pick concrete thresholds for the red-team script to trip. Any suggestions?
[08:21] Evan: Eviction-rate > 500 evictions/min per pool, KV miss-rate > 40% sustained for 2 minutes, p99.9 token latency > 3s for 2 minutes. If two of three are true escalate.
[08:36] Lina: Those numbers sound plausible for canary; for prod the absolute numbers differ by pool size. We'll parameterize thresholds.
[08:43] Jordan: Action item: Priya to formalize thresholds and red-team script. Lina to instrument metrics. Marcus to prototype staged-response. Aisha to coordinate compliance review.
[08:54] Priya: For the tabletop, do we want to do a partial blackout simulation where we disable a model kernel to see fallback?
[09:01] Marcus: Yes, kernel-level fault injection is important, but do it on canary cluster first. The script should include a kernel-slow path toggle.
[09:09] Diego: Network flakiness might be the more realistic failure; we can add 100ms latency to cross-region requests during the sim.
[09:15] Jordan: Good. Timeline — we aim to run the red-team on 2026-11-16. Deliverables before that: script, metrics, and the prototype.
[09:24] Evan: On the day, oncall will run the scenario and record timelines and human actions for the after-action review.
[09:29] Priya: We'll also include an attestation checklist for compliance that disk fallback encryption is in place.
[09:34] Jordan: Anything else?
[09:36] Aisha: One more thing — runbook automations. Can we automate first-level mitigation like retention increases via safe toggles so human error is reduced?
[09:45] Marcus: We can, but restrict to ops role and include a rate-limit on toggles.
[09:50] Priya: We'll prototype that as a playbook command with audit logs.
[09:54] Jordan: Great. Quick parking lot: cost model for disk-backed fallback, legal data residency check, and canary thresholds. We'll capture those as action items.
[10:05] Speaker 6: Might be worth a quick note about customer opt-outs — enterprise customers may want to opt out of disk fallback.
[10:12] Jordan: Yes add that.
[10:14] Evan: Last thing — we should publish an incident runbook revision with clear rollbacks and have it staged in a docs PR before the tabletop.
[10:22] Jordan: OK we're at the end. Recap and owners: Priya (script+thresholds), Lina (metrics), Marcus (prototype), Aisha (stakeholders/compliance), Jordan (schedule and invites). Red-team run 2026-11-16.
[10:37] Priya: I'll send the initial script today and a follow-up by Monday.
[10:42] Jordan: Thanks everyone. Meeting adjourned.
[10:45] Transcript notes: occasional transcription errors present; some speaker labels are generic. Links referenced: doc://red-team/failure-matrix (shared after meeting), dashboard://eviction-gates (dashboard will be created).
